intro: Friedman wrote for three audiences at once: for economists in the journals and monographs that won the Nobel Prize, for the public in Newsweek, the Wall Street Journal and the books written with Rose, and for policymakers in testimony, memoranda and open letters. The Collected Works of Milton Friedman at the Hoover Institution gathers most of it in one place.

items.title: Income from Independent Professional Practice
items.kind: Monograph, with Simon Kuznets · NBER
items.summary: The study of doctors', lawyers' and dentists' incomes that served as his doctoral dissertation. Its finding that medical licensing restricted entry and raised fees was controversial enough to delay publication by several years.

items.title: Roofs or Ceilings? The Current Housing Problem
items.kind: Pamphlet, with George J. Stigler · Foundation for Economic Education
items.summary: A short, sharp case against rent control: price ceilings produce shortages, and the market, not rationing, allocates housing to those who value it most. His first venture into public advocacy.

items.title: Essays in Positive Economics
items.kind: Essays · University of Chicago Press
items.summary: Includes The Methodology of Positive Economics, The Case for Flexible Exchange Rates and The Effects of a Full-Employment Policy on Economic Stability. The methodology essay is among the most cited pieces ever written on economic method.

items.title: Studies in the Quantity Theory of Money
items.kind: Edited volume · University of Chicago Press
items.summary: Papers from the Chicago money workshop, opened by his own restatement of the quantity theory as a theory of the demand for money.

items.title: A Theory of the Consumption Function
items.kind: Monograph · Princeton University Press, for the NBER
items.summary: The permanent income hypothesis. Consumption depends on expected lifetime income, not current income, which explains why saving rates look stable over the long run and why temporary tax changes do little to stimulate spending.

items.title: A Program for Monetary Stability
items.kind: Lectures · Fordham University Press
items.summary: The Millar Lectures. Proposes a constant-growth rule for the money supply, 100 percent reserve banking and the abolition of discretionary monetary policy.

items.title: Capitalism and Freedom
items.kind: Book, with the assistance of Rose D. Friedman · University of Chicago Press
items.summary: The role of competitive capitalism in preserving political freedom, followed by chapters on money, international trade, fiscal policy, education, discrimination, monopoly, licensing, income distribution, welfare and poverty. Over half a million copies sold; new editions in 1982, 2002 and 2020.

items.title: Price Theory: A Provisional Text
items.kind: Textbook · Aldine
items.summary: Lecture notes from his graduate price theory course, taken down by students and revised. The expanded 1976 edition remains in print.

items.title: A Monetary History of the United States, 1867–1960
items.kind: Monograph, with Anna Jacobson Schwartz · Princeton University Press, for the NBER
items.summary: Nearly nine hundred pages tracing the stock of money through greenbacks, the gold standard, the founding of the Federal Reserve, the Great Contraction of 1929 to 1933 and the war. The Nobel committee cited it; Ben Bernanke called it the leading and most persuasive explanation of the worst economic disaster in American history.

items.title: Dollars and Deficits: Inflation, Monetary Policy and the Balance of Payments
items.kind: Essays · Prentice-Hall
items.summary: Collected essays and lectures on living with inflation, the balance of payments and the price of gold.

items.title: The Optimum Quantity of Money and Other Essays
items.kind: Essays · Aldine
items.summary: The title essay introduces the helicopter drop as a thought experiment about how new money enters an economy, and argues that the optimum policy is a mild deflation equal to the real rate of interest. Also includes The Role of Monetary Policy.

items.title: Monetary Statistics of the United States
items.kind: Monograph, with Anna J. Schwartz · NBER
items.summary: The data behind the Monetary History: definitions, sources and estimates of the money stock since 1867.

items.title: An Economist's Protest: Columns in Political Economy
items.kind: Collected columns · Thomas Horton
items.summary: The first collection of Newsweek columns, on everything from the draft and the oil import quota to the price of gold.

items.title: There's No Such Thing as a Free Lunch
items.kind: Collected columns · Open Court
items.summary: A second collection of columns and essays. The title phrase, which Friedman popularised rather than coined, became shorthand for his whole approach.

items.title: Free to Choose: A Personal Statement
items.kind: Book, with Rose D. Friedman · Harcourt Brace Jovanovich
items.summary: The companion to the PBS series and the best-selling non-fiction book in the United States in 1980. The power of the market, the tyranny of controls, the anatomy of crisis, the cradle-to-grave welfare state, created equal, what's wrong with our schools, who protects the consumer and the worker, the cure for inflation, and the tide is turning.

items.title: Monetary Trends in the United States and the United Kingdom
items.kind: Monograph, with Anna J. Schwartz · University of Chicago Press, for the NBER
items.summary: The third volume of the money project, comparing a century of monetary data in the two countries.

items.title: Bright Promises, Dismal Performance: An Economist's Protest
items.kind: Collected columns · Harcourt Brace Jovanovich
items.summary: Columns from 1972 to 1983, edited by William R. Allen.

items.title: Tyranny of the Status Quo
items.kind: Book, with Rose D. Friedman · Harcourt Brace Jovanovich
items.summary: Why the first six to nine months of a new administration are its only chance to change course, and how the iron triangle of politicians, bureaucrats and beneficiaries blocks reform thereafter.

items.title: Money Mischief: Episodes in Monetary History
items.kind: Book · Harcourt Brace Jovanovich
items.summary: The stone money of Yap, the Crime of 1873, William Jennings Bryan, the Federal Reserve's purchase of silver and what it did to China: monetary history as detective story.

items.title: Two Lucky People: Memoirs
items.kind: Memoir, with Rose D. Friedman · University of Chicago Press
items.summary: Their joint autobiography, written in alternating voices and drawing on letters and diaries. Candid on Chile, Nixon, Reagan, the Nobel and sixty years of marriage.

items.title: A Monetary and Fiscal Framework for Economic Stability
items.kind: American Economic Review 38 (June 1948)
items.summary: An early proposal to replace discretionary policy with automatic rules: 100 percent reserves, a balanced budget over the cycle and money creation tied to the deficit.

items.title: The Methodology of Positive Economics
items.kind: Essay, in Essays in Positive Economics
items.summary: Economics should be judged as a positive science by the success of its predictions. The realism of assumptions is not the test; the question is whether the world behaves as if the assumptions held. The billiard-player analogy and the leaves-on-a-tree example come from here.

items.title: The Case for Flexible Exchange Rates
items.kind: Essay, in Essays in Positive Economics
items.summary: Written in Paris in 1950. Floating rates would let countries pursue independent monetary policies and adjust to shocks without the crises that fixed rates invite. The world moved to floating rates after 1973.

items.title: The Role of Government in Education
items.kind: Essay, in Economics and the Public Interest, ed. Robert A. Solo · Rutgers University Press
items.summary: Separates the financing of schooling, which government may justifiably provide, from its administration, which it need not. Proposes vouchers redeemable at any approved school.

items.title: The Quantity Theory of Money: A Restatement
items.kind: Essay, in Studies in the Quantity Theory of Money
items.summary: The demand for money is a stable function of a few variables, which makes the quantity of money the key to the price level and nominal income.

items.title: The Demand for Money: Some Theoretical and Empirical Results
items.kind: Journal of Political Economy 67 (August 1959)
items.summary: Estimates the demand for money using permanent income and finds it stable over long periods, the empirical pillar of monetarism.

items.title: Money and Business Cycles
items.kind: With Anna J. Schwartz · Review of Economics and Statistics 45 (February 1963)
items.summary: Changes in the money stock lead changes in output, with long and variable lags, which is why fine-tuning fails.

items.title: Inflation: Causes and Consequences
items.kind: Lecture · Council for Economic Education, Bombay · Asia Publishing House
items.summary: The source of the line inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon, in the sense that it is and can be produced only by a more rapid increase in the quantity of money than in output.

items.title: The Role of Monetary Policy
items.kind: AEA presidential address · American Economic Review 58 (March 1968)
items.summary: Monetary policy cannot peg interest rates or unemployment for long. There is a natural rate of unemployment; attempts to hold unemployment below it produce accelerating inflation. The most influential paper of his career.

items.title: The Optimum Quantity of Money
items.kind: Essay, in The Optimum Quantity of Money and Other Essays
items.summary: The helicopter-money thought experiment, and the argument that the welfare-maximising policy drives the nominal interest rate to zero.

items.title: The Social Responsibility of Business Is to Increase Its Profits
items.kind: The New York Times Magazine, 13 September 1970
items.summary: Executives who spend shareholders' money on social ends are imposing taxes and deciding how to spend them, functions that belong to government. The doctrine is argued over to this day.

items.title: Prohibition and Drugs
items.kind: Newsweek, 1 May 1972
items.summary: His first public call to end drug prohibition, by analogy with the failure of alcohol prohibition.

items.title: Inflation and Unemployment
items.kind: Nobel lecture, 13 December 1976 · Journal of Political Economy 85 (June 1977)
items.summary: Extends the natural-rate hypothesis: high and variable inflation adds uncertainty and distorts prices, so that in the short run higher inflation may bring higher, not lower, unemployment.

items.title: An Open Letter to Bill Bennett
items.kind: The Wall Street Journal, 7 September 1989
items.summary: To the first director of the Office of National Drug Control Policy: the war on drugs is doing more harm than the drugs, and the policy is incompatible with a free society.

items.title: Why Money Matters
items.kind: The Wall Street Journal, 17 November 2006
items.summary: His last published article, printed the day after his death, on the relation between money growth and the price level in the United States, the United Kingdom and Japan.

items.title: Newsweek column
items.kind: Fortnightly, then three-weekly, 1966–1984
items.summary: More than three hundred columns, alternating with Paul Samuelson and Henry Wallich, on inflation, taxes, the draft, welfare, education, exchange rates, licensing and the Federal Reserve. Collected in An Economist's Protest, There's No Such Thing as a Free Lunch and Bright Promises, Dismal Performance, and fully reproduced in the Hoover Collected Works.

items.title: The Wall Street Journal, The New York Times and others
items.kind: Op-eds and letters, 1960s–2006
items.summary: Dozens of articles over four decades, including the open letter on drugs, the obituary for Friedrich Hayek, articles on the euro and Hong Kong, and the final piece on money.

items.title: Free to Choose and Tyranny of the Status Quo television scripts
items.summary: Thirteen hour-long broadcasts with Rose, each pairing a filmed documentary with a studio debate. Transcripts are available from the Free To Choose Network.
